transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, hi. Um… I guess the main reason is at work I keep getting up from my workstation, even when I know I’m supposed to stay there and finish reviewing claims. I work in insurance claims stuff, so it’s not like I can just wander off whenever—there are these queues and reviews I’m supposed to get through.

But I’ll stand up to get water, or check something, or just… I don’t know, move around, and then suddenly I’m not at my desk. It sounds kind of small when I say it out loud, but it’s been happening enough that it’s becoming a problem. And my desk setup isn’t even bad—I mean, I got this chair that was supposed to help my back, but that’s not really the point. The point is I’m supposed to stay put and finish the claim reviews, and I keep leaving my station.

When you feel the urge to get up from your desk, is it usually because you're preoccupied with worried thoughts about something, or does it happen even when your mind isn't focused on any particular worry?

It’s not usually like I’m sitting there worrying about one specific thing, no. I mean, sometimes work itself is stressful, obviously, because claims can get backed up and then everyone’s watching the numbers, but the getting up happens even when I’m not, like, spiraling about something.

It’s more just… I’m supposed to stay at my workstation and get through the claim reviews, and I’ll still find myself standing up and leaving my desk. Like I know I need to stay put, but I don’t.

Aside from getting up and moving around, do you also notice things like losing your train of thought while reviewing a claim, making careless mistakes, or having trouble keeping your attention on a task even when you're sitting still?

Yeah, I do lose the thread a lot. Like I’ll be reading through a claim note, and if people near me start talking about some other claim, my brain just kind of… goes with that instead. Or I’ll suddenly remember I need to do some random errand after work, like return something or pay a bill, and then I’m still looking at the screen but I’m not really taking in what I’m reading.

Then I have to go back and reread the same section a few times, which is frustrating because it’s not like the claim is that complicated every time. It’s just my attention slides off it.
Thinking back, did you notice similar problems with staying seated, restlessness, or losing focus when you were a child or teenager, say before age 12?

Yeah… I think it goes back pretty far. I don’t remember every detail, obviously, but in elementary school my report cards or teacher comments would say stuff like I was bright, but I’d lose worksheets or miss instructions.

My mom used to keep a folder of school papers, actually, and there were all these notes about needing reminders to finish classwork. I remember that part because it was kind of annoying—I felt like I understood the material, but I’d still somehow not turn things in or not hear what we were supposed to do. So yeah, it wasn’t brand new when I started working.
Do you notice these same problems—getting up, losing focus, forgetting things—outside of work too, like at home or in social situations?

Um… I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, at home it’s kind of harder to tell because nobody’s tracking whether I’m staying in one spot the way they do at work.

Like if I get up while I’m watching TV, is that a problem or just me grabbing water? I don’t really know. And socially… I guess I haven’t paid close attention to it. My friends are pretty casual, we’ll be talking and then someone checks their phone or gets food or whatever, so it doesn’t stand out the same way.

So I can’t say for sure. Work is where I notice it the most because there’s a specific thing I’m supposed to be doing.

Can you think of a specific time recently at home—like paying bills, doing chores, or finishing a task you started—where losing focus or getting up mid-task actually caused a problem, like something not getting done or a mistake happening?

At home… I’m trying to think of a clean example, but honestly the ones that jump out are more work-related. Like, I’ll mean to return a claimant’s call after I finish one thing, and then I’ll get pulled into something else, or just… I don’t know, the thought disappears.

Same with updating a diary note or sending a form—I’ll have it in my head like, “Okay, do that before lunch,” and then later I realize I never did it. It’s embarrassing because it’s usually not hard stuff. It’s simple follow-up things, but I forget them more than I want to admit.
Can you think of a recent time at home—like paying a bill late, forgetting an appointment, or leaving a chore unfinished—where losing focus or getting up mid-task actually caused a real problem?

I’m trying to think of a home example, but the honest answer is the clearest stuff is still at work. Like I’ll mean to do something simple—return a claimant’s call, update a diary note, send a form I already had pulled up—and then I get sidetracked or stand up to do one little thing, and later I’m like, “Wait, I never did that.”

It’s not usually complicated work, which is what makes it frustrating. It’s more like basic follow-up stuff I meant to do earlier that day, and I forget it more than I really want to admit.
Has anyone close to you—like a partner, roommate, or family member—ever commented that you seem distracted, forgetful, or restless at home, even if you haven't noticed it yourself?

Not really in a clear way at home, I guess. I mean, nobody’s said, “You’re distracted,” like that.

The thing I notice more is at work—like if people near me start talking about another claim, or I suddenly remember some random errand I need to do, my attention just kind of slides off what I’m reading. Then I realize I got through the paragraph but didn’t actually take it in, so I have to reread the same section a few times.

At home, I don’t know if anyone would notice it the same way. It’s less obvious, I think.

Besides getting up from your desk, do you notice other signs of restlessness—like fidgeting with your hands or feet, feeling like you need to keep moving, talking more than others in conversations, or blurting out answers or interrupting people before they finish speaking?

Yeah, I think the fidgeting part, definitely. Like in trainings or the longer team meetings, I’ll be sitting there trying to look like I’m paying attention, but my leg is bouncing the whole time, or I’m clicking a pen, or I keep shifting around in the chair.

Sometimes I don’t even notice I’m doing it until I realize the pen clicking is probably annoying someone, so I stop… and then five minutes later I’m doing something else, like moving my foot. It’s more that than, like, blurting things out.
Outside of work, is there any activity you personally care about—like reading a book, following a recipe, or working on a hobby—where you notice yourself losing focus or leaving the task unfinished?

Yeah, I mean… outside work I’m trying to think of a good example. It’s not as clear as at my desk, honestly.

The main thing I notice is still when I’m reading something, even if it’s not for work sometimes. Like if people nearby start talking, or I suddenly remember some random errand I need to do, my attention just kind of slides off the page. Then I realize I technically read the paragraph, but I didn’t actually absorb any of it, so I have to go back and reread the same section a few times.

It’s annoying because I’ll be sitting there like, “Okay, focus,” and then my brain is already somewhere else.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports childhood-onset (before age 12) and persistent symptoms of both inattention (difficulty sustaining attention while reading/reviewing claims, losing train of thought, forgetting to complete follow-up tasks, careless rereading) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (inability to remain seated at workstation, leg bouncing, pen clicking, restlessness in meetings). Symptoms are present in at least two settings (work and to a lesser extent leisure/reading activities), cause functional impairment at work, and were corroborated by childhood school records noting inattentiveness and incomplete work. The combination of significant inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms meeting duration and cross-setting criteria supports a Combined Presentation (F90.2) rather than a single predominant subtype.
